title: The readings and the psalm
hook: Sundays run a three-year cycle so most of the Bible is read aloud

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gloria, the angels' song, silent in Advent and Lent. Your line was glory to God in the highest. What good thing did you praise? Day one hundred and eight.

The Gloria ends, the priest says a short opening prayer, and everyone sits down. That's the signal. The first part of the Mass, the gathering and the mercy and the praise, is over. Now comes the second: listening. A person walks up to a stand called the ambo. Very often it isn't the priest. It's a parishioner, a teacher or a retired mailman or a nervous sixteen-year-old, reading from a big book to a room full of people. And the passage they read wasn't chosen by the priest that week, or by them. It was chosen decades ago, for this exact Sunday, by a plan that runs across three years. Today's word is the name of that book.
screen: `EVERYONE SITS.` → `A PARISHIONER AT THE AMBO.` → `CHOSEN DECADES AGO.`

segments.voice: Lectionary comes from the Latin lectio, a reading. It's the book of readings for Mass, laid out day by day. At the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s, the bishops asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up much more richly to the people. So a new lectionary was built, and it came into use in 1970. Here's how it works on a Sunday. There are four readings, counting the psalm. First, usually from the Old Testament, chosen to echo the Gospel of the day. Then a psalm, sung or said: a cantor sings the verses, and everyone answers with a short refrain. Then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles, often Paul. Then the Gospel. And the Sundays run in a three-year cycle. Year A reads mostly from Matthew. Year B, Mark. Year C, Luke. John comes in around the great seasons, Lent and Easter, and fills out the short year of Mark. So over three years of Sundays, a Catholic who comes every week hears the Gospels in turn and a wide sweep of the rest of the Bible. Not every word, but far more than before the reform, when one year of readings repeated over and over. Weekdays have their own cycle. And on any given Sunday, Roman Rite parishes around the world, in many languages, are reading the same passages. At the end of each reading, the reader says, in the old Latin, Verbum Domini, the word of the Lord. And the people answer, Deo gratias, thanks be to God.
screen: `LECTIO: A READING.` · `FOUR READINGS ON A SUNDAY.` · `YEAR A, B, C.` · `THE SAME PASSAGES, WORLDWIDE.` · then, large: `THANKS BE TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear one line. Settle, and breathe. Here's a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." Let it sit. Say it again in your head, slower. Notice which word catches. Lamp. Feet. Paths. You don't have to decide what it means. Just carry it for a minute. If you pray, you can let it become your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Lectionary. The book of readings for Mass, laid out so that over three years of Sundays, a wide sweep of the Bible is read aloud. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, in turns. Today, look up this coming Sunday's readings. They're easy to find online. Read just one of them before Sunday comes. Day one hundred and eight.

howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, lay readers usually proclaim the first and second readings from the ambo, a cantor leads the responsorial psalm, and the readings follow a three-year cycle (Years A, B and C) shared by Roman Rite parishes worldwide.

original.note: Latin: a reading, the root of lectionary and of lecture.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone reads a bit of the Bible at church.
what it means: a planned book of readings, four on a Sunday, running on a three-year cycle so a wide sweep of the Bible is heard aloud.
what a scholar hears: the Ordo Lectionum Missae of 1969, answering the Council's call in Sacrosanctum Concilium 51 to open the Bible's treasures more lavishly.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook fixed (the collect comes between the Gloria and sitting down); 'after the Council' corrected to 'at the Council' (Sacrosanctum Concilium 51 is the Council's own text); four readings now 'counting the psalm'; 'a large share of the Bible', 'hundreds of languages' and 'two-year' weekday cycle (true only of first readings) softened; 'Catholic churches worldwide' narrowed to Roman Rite parishes; 'the shortest Gospel' superlative cut; stock 'here's the lovely part' cut.
Douay-Rheims Psalm 118:105 given from memory; confirm.

The index hook says 'most of the Bible is read aloud' and the carry says 'the whole book'. Studies suggest the Sunday cycle covers a minority of the Old Testament and a large share of the Gospels; the script says 'a large share' and 'not every word'. A Keeper may want the index hook softened.
New lectionary promulgated 1969, in use from Advent 1969/1970; weekday first readings on a two-year cycle. Confirm.
Easter season first readings come from Acts rather than the Old Testament; the script says 'usually from the Old Testament'. Confirm.
'Verbum Domini / Deo gratias' Latin acclamations; English responses described, not quoted from ICEL ('Thanks be to God' is a traditional phrase).
